title: STAR stories and behavioral interviews
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Interviewers test for ownership, judgement, collaboration, learning from mistakes and impact.
Situation and Task set the scene in two or three sentences.

Prepare six to eight stories that each fit several questions: a hard outage, a disagreement, a project you led, a mistake, a time you influenced without authority, a time you mentored and a time you made a trade-off with incomplete data.
Say how many users were affected, how long it lasted, what it cost and what improved.
Expect questions such as what would you do differently and what did others think.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The answer that said we thirty times
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A candidate described a large migration and could not say what they personally did.
An operator runs a command such as: grep -o -i -w "we" answer.txt | wc -l
The interviewer asked what the candidate decided and got a vague reply.
The candidate rewrote the story with decisions in the first person: the cutover plan, the rollback criteria and the call to delay a week.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Describing the team and not your own actions.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Communicating technical decisions and design reviews
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: An architecture decision record is one page: the context and constraints, the options considered, the decision, and the consequences including costs.
Start with the problem and goals, then non goals, then the proposal, alternatives and risks.
Send the document in advance and ask people to comment in writing.
Lead with the business effect: cost, risk, time and customer impact.
When the decision is made, support it even if you argued against it.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A decision made three times
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
Two years after a database choice, a new team proposed the same change and the debate restarted.
An operator runs a command such as: git log --oneline --diff-filter=A -- docs/adr | wc -l
No decision record existed, so the context was lost when the authors moved on.
The team introduced a short record template, wrote the missing record from memory and linked it from the repository README so the next debate started from facts.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Starting with the solution and no problem statement.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Influence without authority
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A team that is behind on a deadline will not welcome a request to upgrade a library.
Do small things you said you would do, answer promptly and share credit.
Use data from their own systems: error rates, cost, incident counts.
Provide templates, libraries, pipelines and automation so the secure or reliable path takes less effort than any other.
Escalate only after a direct conversation, and tell the other person first.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The mandate that nobody followed
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A platform team announced that all services must adopt a new logging library by quarter end.
An operator runs a command such as: grep -rl "legacy-logger" services | wc -l
Teams had no time and no help, so most ignored the mandate.
The platform team then offered pull requests that did the migration for ten services, a codemod for the rest and a dashboard that showed adoption by team.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Mandates with no help.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Mentoring and giving feedback
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A mentor helps someone reach their goals by asking questions, sharing experience and opening doors.
State what you observed, the effect it had and what you suggest.
Explain the reason behind a comment and link to a guideline.
Listen to the end, ask for an example and thank the person even if you disagree.
Match the task to the person: stretching but possible.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The review that stopped a junior from asking
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A harsh pull request review made a new engineer stop sharing work until it was finished.
An operator runs a command such as: git log --author=maya --since=2.weeks --oneline | wc -l
The activity drop followed a review with sarcastic comments.
The reviewer apologised, rewrote the comments with reasons and suggestions, and agreed a weekly pairing session.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Giving feedback only at review time.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Leading through incidents
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: The incident commander coordinates and does not debug.
Post updates on a fixed cadence, such as every thirty minutes, even if nothing changed.
You rarely have full information.
After a few hours people make mistakes.
A blameless review asks how the system allowed this to happen, not who caused it.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: An incident with three people debugging and nobody talking
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
For two hours no update went to customers or to management.
An operator runs a command such as: grep -c "STATUS UPDATE" incident-4821.log
Everyone was working on the fix and nobody had the communication role.
A commander was named, updates went out every thirty minutes and a rollback that had been delayed was done within ten minutes of the decision.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: The commander debugging as well.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Senior and staff scope and career growth
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A senior engineer delivers complex work independently and improves the team.
Early in a career you are given tasks.
Look for work that many people reuse or that removes a recurring pain: a tool, a standard, a clear document or a hard migration.
Write short summaries of what you did and its effect, share them with your manager and peers, and speak at internal events.
Pick one or two skills for the next six months, such as writing design documents or leading incidents.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The engineer who worked hard and was not promoted
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A strong engineer delivered many tickets for two years and was told they were not ready for staff.
An operator runs a command such as: git shortlog -sn --since=2.years | head -2
Devon was the top contributor, but all the work stayed inside one team and none of it was written up.
After talking to their manager they picked a cross team reliability project, wrote a design document, kept an impact record and were promoted the following year.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Waiting to be noticed.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
